title: Workshop: The Open Agentic Stack: Building the Future of AI Systems with Open Source, Open Standards

segments.text: MATT WHITE: So thanks for having us today here.
I'm the former global CTO of AI at the Linux Foundation.
I previously led the PyTorch Foundation
as the executive director and CTO.
And I'm a visiting scholar at Columbia University.
So before we begin, I would like to share some thoughts
as we are living through unprecedented times.
AI capabilities are advancing at a pace
that would have sounded implausible
only a few years ago.
Models can reason across long contexts,
write and execute code, use tools,
and operate software, and coordinate
increasingly complex workflows.
We are entering a world where powerful models can solve
complex mathematical proofs, generate extensive code bases,
and power systems that take actions in production networks
that have real world impact.
But exactly at this moment when AI
is becoming more capable and more consequential,
openness is under genuine pressure.
So the idea of restricting or even
banning access to open weight models
is no longer a hypothetical.
It's being actively debated in Washington and elsewhere.
And we're also hearing proposals to attempt
to control the frontier through chips, compute, distillation,
safety testing, and model release processes.
The safety and security and national security concerns
behind these discussions are real and legitimate.
They deserve serious, technically-informed responses.
But we must also be equally clear
about the risks on the other side.
Blunt restrictions can concentrate capability,
infrastructure, and decision-making
to a very small number of institutions.
They can transform artificial intelligence
from broadly accessible and general purpose technology
into something that the rest of society
is only permitted to rent from a few labs.
That cannot be the foundation on which we build the future.
Openness is how we create competition.
It is how researchers inspect systems, developers adapt them,
students learn, enterprises maintain sovereignty
over their data and stack, and countries build AI capabilities
without being permanently dependent on a single vendor.
So openness is also an essential part of safety.
It enables reproducible evaluation,
transparent interfaces, independent scrutiny,
shared security tooling, and the ability
to identify and correct problems.
Oh, there's no slides.
It's just me rambling.
But open communities allow more people
to test assumptions, discover vulnerabilities, compare
approaches, and contribute to solutions.
But openness does not mean ungoverned.
It does not mean being careless, unsafe, or a free for all.
Openness means that systems can be inspected, evaluated,
adapted, and improved.
It means that interfaces are interoperable,
implementations are contestable, and no single organization
controls every layer or decides who is permitted to participate.
This becomes even more important as we move into agentic AI,
because an agent is not simply a model.
An agent is a stack.
It includes the model, the harness, the tools that
can invoke the environment in which it acts,
guardrails the reinforcement learning
systems through which it improves,
the evaluation infrastructure that measures it,
and the compute on which the entire systems rely.
An agent may depend on APIs, credentials, sandboxes, memory,
inference systems, orchestration frameworks, and multiple forms
of specialized hardware.
It may cross-organizational, cloud, and geographic boundaries
while completing a single task.
If any one of these layers becomes closed and vertically
controlled, the entire ecosystem becomes less portable, less
competitive, and more fragile.
That is why open models alone are not enough.
We also need open environments, so that agentic tasks
can be reproduced and shared.
We need open reinforcement learning frameworks,
so that more people can improve models and agents.
We need open compute layers, so workloads are not
captive to one cloud or compute vendor.
And we need open standards, so all of these components
can work together without requiring permission
from a central platform.
The open agentic stack is therefore not one project,
it's not one framework or one model,
it is a shared architecture built
from open source software, open standards,
and composable components.
And that is the arc of today's workshop.
We will examine four foundational layers
of that stack--
environments, models, reinforcement learning,
and compute.
Each talk addresses a different technical challenge,
but they share a common principle--
the future of AI should be modular rather than monolithic,
interoperable rather than captive,
and open to participation rather than controlled by permission.
This is not simply a philosophical reference,
it is an architectural, economic, and strategic
requirement for a healthy AI ecosystem.
So thank you for being here.
And thank you for contributing to that future.
With that, we will begin with our first speaker,
Ben Burtenshaw.
[APPLAUSE]
So Ben is from Hugging Face.
Ben will introduce OpenEnv, an open standard and community hub
for building, sharing, and running agentic environments.
These environments define the tools, APIs, credentials,
execution context, and tasks through which
agents learn and operate.
Ben will explain why shared environment specifications
and harness protocols are essential
for reproducible training, safer execution, and collaboration
across the open source ecosystem.
So with that, please welcome Ben to the stage.
BEN BURTENSHAW: Hi, everyone.
So as you heard, I'm Ben from Hugging Face.
And I'm going to talk to you about a project called
OpenEnv and open source agentic RL environments in general.
My opinion, my hypothesis is that RL environments
are the best way to democratize AI, the best way
to take a stake in AI, mainly because they're
pretty easy to build.
They're just applications.
They're just the things that we do on a daily basis.
And for that reason, everyone can get involved.
So I'll work through this in a pretty high level and ecosystem
perspective.
And then Daniel is going to go even deeper on RL.
And we're going to go quite far in it.
But if I miss anything, please come and ask me
questions afterwards or contact me.
So what is an RL environment?
The simplest way to explain what an RL environment is,
is that it's a world that an actor acts within
or an agent acts within.
The original RL environment would be a chess game,
where the board is the world, the pieces
are the state of the environment,
the rules are the actions or the moves
that you can make within the game,
and the game score is the reward.
And in reinforcement learning, we
would use that reward to update our agent
and to learn from that.
So that's just a game, but let's scale that up now to something
a bit more realistic.
So we could take software engineering.
If we say that software engineering is defined
as a task that's in a GitHub issue,
and the work is in the GitHub pull request,
and the score of that work are the results of the test
suite and maybe the CI, then we would
say that we have an environment that's
there for software engineering.
And this is how papers like SWE-smith and others
have built software engineering environments.
We could take this, and we could remove the code from the pull
request and get an agent to generate
a code in that same environment, and use that test suite
to get our reward.
And then we have an environment for software engineering
that we could use to train a software engineering agent.
We could carry that archetype across many different tasks--
email, triage, or say, project management.
And we would need to find the tasks, the reward, and the stay
within those environments, and build them into applications.
And so this is what we're talking
about with RL environments.
So what does the ecosystem look like?
So to explain this, I like to go back
to something called the matter cycle.
If you studied machine learning at school,
you would have encountered it.
It's the model-- annotate, train, test,
evaluate, revise loop.
And it's not so common nowadays because it's
a little bit outdated for modern machine learning.
And we need to update it a bit.
So I like to update it to what I call a capability cycle.
So if we look at a capability cycle,
we would say that we discover capabilities,
we then benchmark them, we represent them in data,
and then we train models on them.
Typically, we discover a capability with a harness
or with some kind of prompt.
We elicit this capability out of the model.
And we can see that, OK, it is able to do a certain thing,
maybe not reliably.
We can then evaluate that capability.
And we'll typically use another software stack for that.
And we'll have an evaluation harness
that will measure this capability in the model and how
frequent, how reliable it is.
And we can iterate upon that as a community.
Next, we'll want to represent that firstly, as a data set,
and then eventually, as an environment.
And that's where domain expertise will come into this.
And so companies like Merkle will
do a great job of building reinforcement learning
environments around capabilities, for which they'll
go out, and speak to, and hire domain experts
in their respective domain, and build that environment that
encapsulates that capability, partially based
on the benchmark, but ideally, without any form of leakage
between the two.
And we'll then have a means that we can train a model on.
And so that's when the trainers will come in,
another part of the software stack but also
another community.
Right now, we'll have labs that are training models
using these data sets and environments.
So what you can see from this capability cycle
is that environments are the means with which
that we move capabilities from domain experts into the models
that we use.
And once the models and harnesses have these abilities,
then we move on to the next one.
And we know that this capability is in the weights, as it were.
So that's a really high level view.
What you'll take from that cycle is
that there are many moving parts,
many different communities all playing in on the environment.
And therefore, it's a really important part
of the stack to be open.
This is the means with which that we're
communicating capabilities.
Imagine if data sets were in a closed format,
it would be a particularly horrible situation.
And that's the goal of OpenEnv.
So if you look for environments, you'll typically
go to papers and GitHub, and you'll
find that they're very distributed.
If you look at the recent Kimi K3 paper,
it came with thousands of environments.
The MiniMax paper had, I think, 10,000 environments.
Even the first DeepSeek paper had roughly 1,000 environments.
And all of these implemented in different ways.
Some of them are shared in different ways, many of them
are sold.
And they're not something that's readily available in the way
that open weight models are.
It reminds me a lot of being an MLE back in, say,
2017, when you would find implementations for models
on GitHub, and then you'd go to Google Drive,
and you'd find the weights from there.
And nothing is really exposed and interoperable in the way
that it is today with model checkpoints.
So that's the problem.
And then that problem compounds when
you start to look at training.
Daniel's going to go into this in more detail,
but at a high level, a training process is a framework.
We have a library like TRL or Unsloth
that we use to update our model based on some kind of action
that it does.
And in this context, we want to use an agent harness
to perform the task.
So let's say, it's the software engineering task.
That agent harness is going to do that and interact
with this environment, use tools in that environment.
And then we're going to update the model.
So at each of these edges, we have a different layer
that needs to be interfaced.
And we can't have a harness that expects a certain environment
definition.
And we need to also work with multiple harnesses like Pi,
and Codex, and Claude Code, et cetera.
So the challenge compounds.
One of the main mechanisms that we're
working on in OpenEnv to get this to work
are environment hubs.
So on Hugging Face, we have about 4,000 environments now
that can be pooled in a standard format,
that you can plug into most major training frameworks.
There are other environment hubs, like Prime Intellect.
And there are also more coming.
And we're collaborating with orgs
to share our specs, so that if they build environment hubs,
they'll be able to use a spec such that they
can download environments and share them in an easy way.
So in code terms, this is what it looks like to use OpenEnv.
We imagine that it would mainly be driven by an agent,
but it's a bit like Docker.
So you'd say, openenv init, and you
would get a scaffold of a Hello World environment
that just gives you a generic score.
And from that, you would just need
to write the business logic for your environment,
or you could generate the business logic
with a code agent.
You could also import environments
from different libraries, like verifiers.
And then you can push, pull, and fork environments on the hub,
so that you can share them or use
other people's and adapt them.
That's the base layer of OpenEnv.
And the features that we're working on next
are to be able to discover environments from hubs
and then to be able to validate them.
So at the moment, the process of finding
an environment for your use case is quite difficult.
But if you could search for environments on the hub,
you'd be able to pull those and get
a range of community environments, which
is quite nice.
We can share with each other.
And then that creates another challenge, how do I know
which environment is better?
How do I know which environment is going to help on my use case?
And that's where this new validate command comes in,
where we'll say, OK, this is a valid spec.
And also, we can train a small model
to see if it lifts performance on a given benchmark.
So with these two commands we'll have
an autonomous loop for integrating environments
in post-training.
So the last block of the talk is then,
how can I use an RL environment?
So the quickest way to get started would be in evaluation.
And I'd suggest that most people do
this, because you can represent a typical workload
as an environment, and you can see how good a model is.
So you could take a model as weights or as just an API.
And you could define your environment
with a set of tasks and a reward function,
and run the model over those tasks.
And you'd get back an aggregate score
of how good a model is at your environment.
The core way that we would look at this
would be with reinforcement learning.
So we would take a model or a policy.
And we would roll it out over this environment
and get a set of actions.
And then we would calculate rewards
on each of those rollouts.
We could use an algorithm like GRPO, which Daniel, I know,
is going to come into further, where we would calculate
the reward for each of those rollouts
and then take a mean across the whole group,
and update the weights based on that mean.
And then we'd iterate like that.
So if you're interested in more detail on this,
I've got a few talks where I go into greater detail on this,
but at a high level, this is how we'd use an RL environment.
And then the next way would be distillation.
So in this setting, you wouldn't really
be able to distill from strings, you
wouldn't be able to distill from tokens.
You will need log probabilities.
And we would take a student and a teacher model.
We would roll out the student, so we'd
get it to perform a task inside an environment.
And we take the log probabilities
of that student on this task.
And then we would get a teacher to do the same task--
or to roll out over the same token, sorry.
And we take the log probabilities
of the teacher on those tokens, and then update
the weights of the student based on the difference,
the reverse KL from the student and the teacher.
That's one way.
We could do this in a few different ways.
So we could also take the student
and do self-distillation, where we say,
OK, let's take the best example of the student
and compare it to the average.
Or we could give the student some kind
of privileged information or hint.
We might get that from the environment or from a data set.
Like for example, in the pull request setup, we could say,
here's the actual solution to this code.
And we give that to the agent at the beginning.
And then we update the weights based
on the difference between its bad run and its good run.
So that's the core of OpenEnv.
That's what we're working on.
The main takeaway is that we're trying
to make it so that open environments can
be shared openly across the Hugging Face
hub, but also others.
And how do we think that this is going to work?
How do we think it's going to be effective?
The answer to that is leaderboards.
We see environments at the moment existing
in a bit of a shadow realm.
They're not really spoken about that much or they're not
really seen within the community around model releases.
And we think that if people can start
to build their own environments and try them out,
and then we put them into leaderboards,
and we figure out which ones are good
and which ones are contributing to model success,
then more people will get involved,
and we'll share more of these leaderboards.
So that's the talk.
